chapter.title: Amino Acids, Peptides, and Proteins
chapter.scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT biochemistry lessons covering the declared outline sections. This release is implemented, not independently scientifically verified; it is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: Protein amino acids share an alpha carbon attached to an amino group, a carboxyl group, hydrogen and a side chain. Side-chain chemistry changes polarity, charge and packing.

At near-neutral pH, free amino acids usually have ammonium and carboxylate groups. Aspartate and glutamate tend to be negative; lysine and arginine tend to be positive. Histidine protonation depends strongly on its environment.
Glycine has two hydrogens at its alpha carbon and is achiral. Protein amino acids are predominantly L; L does not mean that every alpha center has an S configuration.
Two cysteine side chains can form a covalent disulfide on oxidation. Methionine contains sulfur but does not form the same disulfide cross-link.

steps.text: For one ionizable group, pH below its pKa favors the protonated form; pH above its pKa favors the deprotonated form. Count every group before summing net charge.
The isoelectric point is the pH at which the average net charge is zero. For an amino acid without an ionizable side chain, average the two pKa values that bracket its neutral form.
An acidic or basic side chain changes which two pKa values bracket zero charge. Averaging the smallest and largest pKa without checking charge states can give the wrong pI.
A buffer is most effective near a relevant pKa. At pH = pKa, the deprotonated-to-protonated ratio for that group is one; zero net charge does not mean all groups are uncharged.

steps.text: A peptide bond is an amide linkage between a carboxyl-derived carbon and an amino-derived nitrogen. The chain is conventionally read from its N terminus toward its C terminus.
Resonance gives the peptide C–N bond partial double-bond character, making the peptide unit approximately planar. Rotation around the adjacent backbone bonds still permits conformations.
Hydrolysis cleaves the amide using water. Cellular peptide synthesis uses activated substrates and ribosomal machinery; it is not spontaneous dehydration of free amino acids in water.
A linear chain of n amino acids has n minus one peptide bonds. Side chains retain their identities, while most internal backbone amino and carboxyl groups are tied up in amides.

steps.text: Primary structure is the covalent amino-acid sequence. A sequence substitution can change higher-order folding even when chain length remains constant.
Alpha helices and beta sheets are secondary structures stabilized chiefly by hydrogen bonding between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens.
In an alpha helix, side chains project outward. Beta sheets contain aligned strands that may be parallel or antiparallel; side chains alternate above and below the sheet.
Proline and glycine affect conformational preferences, but a sequence motif does not guarantee one fold in every context. Secondary structure is not synonymous with side-chain bonding.

steps.text: Tertiary structure describes the three-dimensional organization of one polypeptide. Hydrophobic burial often favors nonpolar side chains inside soluble proteins.
Hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, dispersion forces and sometimes disulfides help stabilize a fold. Membrane proteins face a different environment from soluble proteins.
Quaternary structure describes association among multiple polypeptide subunits. A functional monomer has tertiary structure without requiring quaternary structure.
Changes at a subunit interface can alter cooperativity or assembly without breaking peptide bonds. Always identify whether a question concerns one chain or a multi-chain complex.

steps.text: Denaturation disrupts a protein’s native higher-order structure and often its function. Heat, extreme pH and certain solvents can disturb stabilizing interactions.
Ordinary denaturation does not by itself mean peptide-bond hydrolysis. Reducing agents specifically disrupt disulfides, whereas detergents can disrupt noncovalent packing.
Some unfolded proteins refold when native conditions return; others aggregate or require assistance. Reversibility depends on sequence, damage and environment.
A loss of activity does not identify the exact structural lesion. Compare activity, solubility and structural measurements before assigning a mechanism.
